rows.notes: The paper is explicitly labelled a Review and its treatment of sub-surface drip irrigation (Section 4.3) is a narrative synthesis of other work (Payero et al., Colaizzi et al., Evett et al.) on water savings and application efficiency; it reports no own trial, survey or validated model on SDI and aquifer lifespan. The only original data handling is a descriptive remote-sensing timeline of normalised soil moisture and GRACE groundwater-storage percentiles for the three HPA regions (Section 3.2, Figure 7), which does not concern SDI. The statement that SDI could extend the aquifer's life is a recommendation drawn from cited literature, not an own result.

Review article; Section 4.2 on soil moisture sensing cites reductions in irrigation water use in Kansas groundwater management districts (Butler et al.), predicted cost savings in Texas (Ogallala Aquifer Program report) and the USDA survey share of farms using sensors, but reports no own measurement or survey of sensor-based scheduling and its effect on groundwater extraction or aquifer lifespan. The own remote-sensing analysis of soil moisture and groundwater-storage percentiles (Section 3.2, Figure 7) describes regional drought and storage trends, not the effect of soil moisture sensors. The claim that sensors could reduce extractions and extend aquifer life is an inference from cited work.

notes: The document is a literature review with a small descriptive remote-sensing component (satellite soil moisture and GRACE groundwater percentiles, 2010-2019) that is not tied to any of the cited technologies. Q1 was answered 'no' because the article is a review and the sections supporting the claims are purely synthesis; even if the remote-sensing component were counted as primary data, Q2 would still be 'no' for both rows since none of that data concerns SDI or soil moisture sensors.
